However, opening the next two negotiation clusters would still depend on Ukraine’s parliament adopting a minority education bill on Oct. 12. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 5, 2026, 5:51 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Hungary?s Prime Minister Peter Magyar speaks during a joint press conference with Ireland's Prime Minister (not in picture) in Budapest, Hungary, on June 4, 2026. (Photo by ATTILA KISBENEDEK / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Hungary is expected to ease its veto on further progress in Ukraine and Moldova’s EU accession talks this week, potentially clearing the way for negotiations on two additional policy clusters. Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar instructed the country’s diplomats not to block letters inviting Kyiv and Chisinau to submit negotiating positions for the next stage of the process, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Monday, Oct. 5, citing two officials. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . The two clusters cover the EU internal market, competitiveness, and inclusive growth. Budapest has repeatedly prevented their advancement because decisions at this stage require the unanimous support of all 27 EU members. The planned move is procedural and does not yet amount to Hungary’s unconditional approval to open the clusters. Budapest’s final political support depends on the Verkhovna Rada adopting legislation expanding education rights for Ukraine’s national minorities. Advertisement “The accession process of Ukraine is taking shape, with due process and a realistic approach,” an EU official familiar with negotiations with Budapest told the FT. Parliament vote remains decisive Ukraine registered the draft education legislation in parliament on Thursday, Oct. 1 and is expected to hold a vote on Monday, Oct. 12. The proposed law would give Hungarian-speaking communities and other national minorities whose languages are official in the EU greater opportunities to receive education in their native languages. Other Topics of Interest Russian Attack Sends Projectile Into Bus at Moldova Border A passenger bus and control booth were damaged at the Palanca crossing during Russia’s Monday attack on Ukraine. Schools where more than half of pupils study in a minority language could receive special status. However, the legislation would not extend the same provisions to Russian as it is not an official EU language. Magyar welcomed the bill, saying it would strengthen legal guarantees for Hungarian-language education and the network of minority schools. Roughly 100,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine, mainly in the western Zakarpattia region. Budapest has long argued that Ukraine’s education legislation restricts their linguistic and cultural rights. Advertisement Kyiv and Budapest reached an agreement in principle on the community’s language, cultural, educational, and political rights in June, but Hungary subsequently blocked the second and third accession clusters . If the Rada approves the bill, EU officials could formally advance the clusters before the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15. Four clusters could be open EU accession negotiations are divided into six thematic clusters containing the reforms a candidate country must complete before joining the bloc. Ukraine and Moldova have so far opened the Fundamentals cluster, which covers the judiciary, democratic institutions, and fundamental rights, as well as the External Relations cluster. Hungary has blocked clusters two and three multiple times , while other EU members opposed separating Moldova from Ukraine and advancing the two countries at different speeds. If the internal market and competitiveness clusters are opened, only two clusters would remain: one addressing green policy and connectivity and the another covering resources, agriculture, and cohesion. The European Commission hopes to open those remaining clusters for Ukraine and Moldova before the end of 2026. Advertisement Opening all six clusters would not mean that either country is able to join the EU. Each cluster contains detailed benchmarks and reforms that must be negotiated, implemented, and eventually closed with the unanimous approval of member states. Magyar has adopted a less confrontational approach toward Ukraine than his predecessor, Viktor Orbán, but has continued to oppose an accelerated accession process. In June, he secured the removal of language calling for faster Ukrainian accession from an EU summit declaration. The expected compromise would allow Magyar to present the education bill as a diplomatic achievement for Hungary’s minority while enabling Ukraine and Moldova to move forward with their membership bids.
